name: Agave
look_here_first: Start with the broad, fleshy, toothed leaves and terminal spine. Compare mature leaf width and the flowering architecture: a branched panicle supports A. americana, while lechuguilla has narrower leaves and a largely spike-like flowering axis.

comparison_cards.title: Agave structural comparisons
comparison_cards.look_here_first: A. lechuguilla: much narrower leaves, typically 30–50 × 2–4(–5.2) cm, and largely spicate inflorescence. Do not diagnose species or local nativity by blue color, variegation, or ornamental occurrence. Other cultivated agaves can overlap; require reproductive/leaf-edge evidence when uncertain. A. americana has much broader leaves and a branched panicle. A. univittata has undulate/crenate, less detachable leaf margins and teeth mostly 1–2 cm apart; overlaps require close leaf-edge and flowering evidence. Hybridization is documented in FNA; avoid size-only identification.
comparison_cards.caution: Use exact structural characters and provenance; source pictures are first-pass recognition views.

part_examples.look_for: Visible broad succulent leaves, toothed margins and pointed tips in cultivated material. Neighboring plants and scape parts are present; do not assign every visible structure to the agave. No scale or complete flowering panicle is shown.

part_examples.title: Texas USDA habit view: basal narrow-leaved rosettes and a tall largely spike-like flowering axis
part_examples.look_for: Visible basal rosettes and tall unbranched-looking flowering axis west of Van Horn, Texas. Older low-resolution photograph; leaf tooth measurements and flower anatomy cannot be read from it.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Look at narrow rigid rosette leaves, their spaced marginal teeth, and the terminal spine; then inspect the largely spike-like flowering axis. Distinguish A. univittata with leaf-edge detail, not size alone.
